Title: Arbitrary Object Deserialization in Remote DevTools HttpRestartServer leading to Remote Code Execution
Analysis:
### Data Flow Trace
1. **Source**: Untrusted HTTP request body accessed via `request.getBody()` in `HttpRestartServer.handle(ServerHttpRequest, ServerHttpResponse)`.
2. **Sanitization/Validation**: None. The bytes from the request body are passed directly into a standard `ObjectInputStream` constructor. There are no object filters (e.g., `ObjectInputFilter`) or restrictions placed on which classes can be deserialized.
3. **Sink**: The binary stream is processed by `objectInputStream.readObject()` on line 74, executing arbitrary code execution if a serializable gadget chain is present on the classpath.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
To trigger this vulnerability, an attacker constructs a serialized gadget chain (such as a CommonsCollections or Spring gadget chain depending on classpath dependencies) and transmits it to the Remote DevTools restart endpoint:

```http
POST /~devtools~/restart HTTP/1.1
Host: target-application.example.com
X-AUTH-TOKEN: <devtools-secret-token>
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Content-Length: <payload-length>

[RAW BINARY SERIALIZED GADGET CHAIN DATA]
```

Although Remote DevTools requires a secret header (`X-AUTH-TOKEN` or similar, depending on configuration) when auto-configured, Java deserialization of untrusted input remains a critical risk. If the secret is weak, leaked, or bypassed, an attacker can completely compromise the host system. Furthermore, no validation of the class type (`ClassLoaderFiles`) is enforced before the deserialization processes the serialized stream, leading to instant gadget execution during the reading phase.
Snippet:
ObjectInputStream objectInputStream = new ObjectInputStream(request.getBody());
			ClassLoaderFiles files = (ClassLoaderFiles) objectInputStream.readObject();
